In summary, our research is concerned with
the first description of the carotenoid composition of two gammarid species, and of the parasite P. minutus.
the carotenoid composition of two freshwater amphipopod species and their acanthocephala parasite, and with the effect of infection on the carotenoid uptake of the host.
the carotenoid metabolism of a parasite, and provides new insights on the carotenoid transfer from a crustacean host to a parasite.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the parasite P. minutus is able to accumulate astaxanthin, but in esterified forms.
the parasite is unable to metabolize the astaxanthin esters, which are the predominant form of carotenoids in Gammarus.
the acanthocephalans, as parasites, are able to modify their carotenoid content, but not the one of their hosts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
carotenoids are not transferred from gammarids to P. minutus.
carotenoids are not a limiting factor in the development of the parasite, but rather that the parasite has the ability to accumulate and store carotenoid esters.
the parasite P. minutus does not seem to be able to use carotenoids from its hosts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
P. minutus parasites do not accumulate xanthophyll pigments from their host, which is in agreement with the fact that the acanthocephalans are not able to synthesize carotenoids de novo.
the carotenoid composition of the parasite differs significantly from that of the host.
the carotenoid composition of gammarids is different from that of their acanthocephalans parasites.
